# Spring Boot Container Diagnostics

This example demonstrates how Java Flight Recorder (JFR), `jcmd`, and Native
Memory Tracking (NMT) behave when a Spring Boot service runs in a container.

The application is the same famous-quotes style Spring Boot application used by
the other workshop examples. That keeps the diagnostic workflow grounded in a
realistic service: a web endpoint, a database-backed repository, application
startup logs, and a JVM that stays alive while it serves requests.

The point is not that full JDK images are always better than slim images. The
point is more precise:

- some diagnostics need command-line tools such as `jcmd`;
- some diagnostics need runtime modules such as `jdk.jfr`;
- some diagnostics need startup flags, such as
  `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`;
- a custom `jlink` runtime must include the diagnostics that the deployment
  model requires.

This is a focused diagnostics example. It intentionally does not cover every
container concern that matters for a production Spring Boot service, such as
non-root users, layered JAR extraction, CDS, Project Leyden AOT cache, SBOMs,
vulnerability scanning, or base-image digest review. For a more holistic
container packaging example, see
[Spring Boot Web Application with all examples in one place](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

Enable `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` in production only when native memory
diagnostics are an expected operational requirement. It has runtime overhead and
must be enabled at JVM startup, so treat it as a deliberate observability
tradeoff, not a default hardening or performance recommendation.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

- `curl`, used to call the Spring Boot endpoint.

- `jq`, used to format the JSON response returned by the application.

- `tree`, used to inspect generated directories in the walkthrough.

- [Oracle Account](https://profile.oracle.com/myprofile/account/create-account.jspx)
  to access [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/).

- An Oracle Container Registry authentication token stored in
  `~/.ocr/auth-token`, or an equivalent secure way to pass the password to
  `docker login --password-stdin`.

## Build the application

Build the application once before creating the container image variants. The
point of the rest of the walkthrough is to compare runtime images, so the
application artefact should stay constant while only the Java runtime changes.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the application

   Run the application locally and request a random quote. This proves that the
   executable JAR works before introducing Dockerfiles, base images, and custom
   runtimes. If this step fails, the problem is in the application build rather
   than in the container diagnostics setup.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the application to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Winston Churchill",
     "id": 189,
     "quote": "Never give in—never, never, never, never, in nothing great or small, large or petty, never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Full JDK diagnostics

Start with the full JDK image because it establishes the diagnostic baseline.
The image is not optimised for size, but it does include the serviceability
tools and runtime modules expected from a JDK distribution. That makes it a
useful control case before removing modules with `jlink`.

This Dockerfile also enables Native Memory Tracking at startup with
`-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`. NMT cannot be enabled after the JVM has
started, so this is a deployment-time decision rather than an emergency command
you can add later with `docker exec`.

1. Review the container image

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   ARG JAR_FILE=./target/container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar

   COPY ${JAR_FILE} app.jar

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

2. Build the full JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Complete-JDK' \
     --tag 'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     '.'
   ```

3. Start the full JDK runtime image.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the container to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Voltaire",
     "id": 172,
     "quote": "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it."
   }
   ```

4. List Java processes with `jcmd`.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd
   ```

   The output shows the Spring Boot JVM and the short-lived `jcmd` process used
   to inspect it. In this container, process `1` is the application JVM.

   ```
   1 app.jar
   56 jdk.jcmd/sun.tools.jcmd.JCmd
   ```

5. Inspect Native Memory Tracking.

   This works because the image has `jcmd` and the JVM was started with
   `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
   ```

   NMT reports native memory reservations and committed memory by JVM subsystem.
   The exact numbers are environment-specific; the important point is that the
   diagnostic command is available and the JVM was started with NMT enabled.


6. Start, inspect, dump, and stop a short JFR recording.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.start name=demo settings=profile
   ```

   The JVM starts a named JFR recording inside the running application process.
   No file is written yet; the recording remains in memory until it is dumped or
   stopped.

   ```
   1:
   Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default.

   Use jcmd 1 JFR.dump name=demo filename=FILEPATH to copy recording data to file.
   ```

   Check the recording status

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.check
   ```

   The recording is running. This is the quick sanity check before waiting long
   enough to collect a few events.

   ```
   1:
   Recording 1: name=demo maxsize=250.0MB (running)
   ```

   Wait a few seconds before dumping the recording so the JVM can collect
   events.

   ```shell
   sleep 10
   ```

   Dump the recording to `/tmp/demo.jfr`

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.dump name=demo filename=/tmp/demo.jfr
   ```

   The JFR file is written inside the container.

   ```
   1:
   Dumped recording "demo", 294.9 kB written to:

   /tmp/demo.jfr
   ```

   Copy the recording out with `docker cp` or write it to a mounted volume
   before removing the container.

   ```shell
   docker cp 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk:/tmp/demo.jfr' './target/complete-jdk.jfr'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Open the recording with the JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/target/complete-jdk.jfr"
   ```

   Stop the recording

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.stop name=demo
   ```

   Stopping the recording releases the in-process JFR recording state after the
   dump has been written.

   ```
   1:
   Stopped recording "demo".
   ```

7. Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-complete-jdk'
   ```

## Minimal runtime tradeoff

A smaller custom runtime is attractive because it removes parts of the JDK that
the application does not need to serve traffic. That is a valid optimisation,
but it has an operational cost: if the runtime omits diagnostic tools or
modules, some incident-response commands cannot run inside the container.

This section intentionally builds a runtime that can run the Spring Boot
application but does not include `jdk.jcmd` or `jdk.jfr`. The failure later in
the section is expected and useful: it shows the tradeoff rather than an
application defect.

1. Review the container image

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS build
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   ARG JAVA_MODULES=java.base,java.compiler,java.desktop,java.instrument,java.management,java.naming,java.sql,java.security.jgss
   ARG JAR_FILE=./target/container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar

   COPY ${JAR_FILE} app.jar

   # binutils are needed by the `--strip-debug` command line option
   RUN dnf install -y binutils && dnf clean all
   RUN jlink \
       --add-modules "${JAVA_MODULES}" \
       --strip-debug \
       --no-header-files \
       --no-man-pages \
       --compress=zip-9 \
       --output /opt/jre

   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   COPY --from=build /opt/jre /opt/jre
   COPY --from=build /opt/app/app.jar app.jar

   # Add the custom runtime tools to PATH so `docker exec ... jcmd` works.
   ENV PATH="/opt/jre/bin:${PATH}"

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

2. Build the smallest custom runtime image.

   This image includes the modules needed by the application, but not the
   diagnostic tool modules used in the previous section.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Slim-JRE' \
     --tag 'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre' \
     '.'
   ```

3. Start the minimal custom runtime image.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre' \
     --publish '8080:8080' \
     'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the container to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "William Shakespeare",
     "id": 180,
     "quote": "All that glitters is not gold."
   }
   ```

4. Try to run `jcmd`.

   The application still responds to HTTP requests, but the runtime no longer
   has the `jcmd` executable. That is exactly the distinction this example is
   meant to make: functional correctness and diagnostic readiness are separate
   properties of a container image.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre' \
     jcmd
   ```

   This should fail because the custom runtime was built without `jdk.jcmd` and
   `jdk.jfr`. That does not mean the application is broken. It means this
   runtime image does not include the diagnostic tools.

   ```
   Error: crun: executable file `jcmd` not found in $PATH: No such file or directory: OCI runtime attempted to invoke a command that was not found
   ```

5. Capture Native Memory Tracking statistics on orderly shutdown.

   `jcmd` is not the only way to retrieve NMT information. The JVM can print a
   final NMT summary to standard output when it exits. This does not require the
   `jdk.jcmd` module, but it is a shutdown-time report rather than an
   interactive diagnostic facility.

   Stop the previous container before starting a separate instance configured to
   print NMT statistics. This instance is deliberately not run with `--rm`,
   because its logs must remain available after it stops.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre'
   ```

   Run the application again with NMT enabled and configure the JVM to print its
   NMT statistics when it exits. `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` passes these options to the
   Java launcher without changing the container image.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --detach \
     --name 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre-shutdown-nmt' \
     --env 'JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS=-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintNMTStatistics' \
     'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre'
   ```

   Stop the container gracefully. `docker stop` sends `SIGTERM` first, allowing
   the JVM to exit and write its final statistics.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre-shutdown-nmt'
   ```

   Read the Native Memory Tracking section from the stopped container’s logs.

   ```shell
   docker logs 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre-shutdown-nmt' 2>&1 \
     | awk '/Native Memory Tracking:/ { found = 1 } found'
   ```

   NMT statistics are written to the container logs even though this runtime
   does not include `jcmd`.

   ```
   Native Memory Tracking:

   Total: reserved=9925773608, committed=608950568
          malloc: 28391720 #12493, peak=28166945 #12495
          mmap:   reserved=9897381888, committed=580558848

   -                 Java Heap (reserved=8292139008, committed=520093696)
                               (mmap: reserved=8292139008, committed=520093696, at peak)

   -                     Class (reserved=1073828981, committed=873589)
                               (classes #1117)
                               (  instance classes #966, array classes #151)
                               (malloc=87157 tag=Class #1425) (peak=87213 #1418)
                               (mmap: reserved=1073741824, committed=786432, at peak)
                               (  Metadata:   )
                               (    reserved=67108864, committed=6815744)
                               (    used=6729776)
                               (    waste=85968 =1.26%)
                               (  Class space:)
                               (    reserved=1073741824, committed=786432)
                               (    used=703024)
                               (    waste=83408 =10.61%)

   -                    Thread (reserved=14740280, committed=912184)
                               (threads #13)
                               (stack: reserved=14680064, committed=851968, peak=851968)
                               (malloc=41016 tag=Thread #109) (peak=49400 #113)
                               (arena=19200 #32) (peak=315976 #30)

   -                      Code (reserved=253769520, committed=7866160)
                               (malloc=136024 tag=Code #2202) (peak=136032 #2203)
                               (mmap: reserved=253632512, committed=7729152, at peak)
                               (arena=984 #1) (peak=34696 #2)

   -                        GC (reserved=213755430, committed=61957670)
                               (malloc=17720870 tag=GC #840) (at peak)
                               (mmap: reserved=196034560, committed=44236800, at peak)

   -                 GCCardSet (reserved=296, committed=296)
                               (malloc=296 tag=GCCardSet #4) (at peak)
   ...
   ```

   This is a limited fallback, not a replacement for live diagnostics. It cannot
   inspect a running JVM or capture baselines and diffs, and it produces no
   report if the container is terminated with `SIGKILL`, including an OOM kill.

6. Remove the stopped container.

   ```shell
   docker rm 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-slim-jre-shutdown-nmt'
   ```

## Diagnostic runtime

The diagnostic custom runtime keeps the image smaller than a full JDK image
while adding back the specific diagnostics used by this example. This is the
more realistic engineering choice when a team wants custom runtimes but still
needs a defined support workflow.

Do not treat `jdk.jcmd` and `jdk.jfr` as a universal module list. They are the
modules needed for this walkthrough. A production service should derive its
runtime modules from the application, framework behaviour, security policy, and
the diagnostics the team actually expects to use.

1. Review the container image

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS build
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   ARG JAVA_MODULES=java.base,java.compiler,java.desktop,java.instrument,java.management,java.naming,java.sql,java.security.jgss,jdk.jcmd,jdk.jfr
   ARG JAR_FILE=./target/container-diagnostics-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar

   COPY ${JAR_FILE} app.jar

   # binutils are needed by the `--strip-debug` command line option
   RUN dnf install -y binutils && dnf clean all
   RUN jlink \
       --add-modules "${JAVA_MODULES}" \
       --strip-debug \
       --no-header-files \
       --no-man-pages \
       --compress=zip-9 \
       --output /opt/jre

   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim
   WORKDIR /opt/app

   COPY --from=build /opt/jre /opt/jre
   COPY --from=build /opt/app/app.jar app.jar

   # Add the custom runtime tools to PATH so `docker exec ... jcmd` works.
   ENV PATH="/opt/jre/bin:${PATH}"

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

2. Build the diagnostic custom runtime image.

   This image adds `jdk.jcmd` and `jdk.jfr` to the application runtime modules.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-Diagnostics-JRE' \
     --tag 'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     '.'
   ```

3. Start the diagnostic custom runtime image.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --name 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     --publish 8080:8080 \
     'demo:container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the container to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Aristotle",
     "id": 24,
     "quote": "Pleasure in the job puts perfection in the work."
   }
   ```

4. List Java processes with `jcmd`.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd
   ```

   The custom runtime now has `jcmd`, so it can list the application JVM just as
   the full JDK image did.

   ```
   1 app.jar
   52 jdk.jcmd/sun.tools.jcmd.JCmd
   ```

5. Inspect Native Memory Tracking.

   This works because the image has `jcmd` and the JVM was started with
   `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary
   ```

   NMT works here for the same two reasons as in the full JDK image: the runtime
   includes `jcmd`, and the JVM was started with
   `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`.

6. Start, inspect, dump, and stop a short JFR recording.

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.start name=demo settings=profile
   ```

   JFR can start because the custom runtime includes the JFR module instead of
   only the minimum modules required to serve HTTP traffic.

   ```
   1:
   Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default.

   Use jcmd 1 JFR.dump name=demo filename=FILEPATH to copy recording data to file.
   ```

   Check the recording status

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.check
   ```

   The recording status confirms that the diagnostic custom runtime supports the
   same JFR workflow as the full JDK image.

   ```
   1:
   Recording 1: name=demo maxsize=250.0MB (running)
   ```

   Wait a few seconds before dumping the recording so the JVM can collect
   events.

   ```shell
   sleep 10
   ```

   Dump the recording to `/tmp/demo.jfr`

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.dump name=demo filename=/tmp/demo.jfr
   ```

   The JFR file is written inside the container.

   ```
   1:
   Dumped recording "demo", 265.2 kB written to:

   /tmp/demo.jfr
   ```

   Copy the recording out with `docker cp` or write it to a mounted volume
   before removing the container.

   ```shell
   docker cp 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre:/tmp/demo.jfr' './target/diagnostics-jre.jfr'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Open the recording with the JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/target/diagnostics-jre.jfr"
   ```

   Stop the recording

   ```shell
   docker exec \
     'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre' \
     jcmd 1 JFR.stop name=demo
   ```

   Stopping the recording completes the same basic JFR lifecycle as the full JDK
   image: start, check, dump, stop.

   ```
   1:
   Stopped recording "demo".
   ```

   7. Stop the container once ready.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'container-diagnostics-spring-boot-diagnostics-jre'
   ```

## What this shows

This example separates three concerns that are easy to blur together:

- A **full JDK image** includes diagnostic tools by default.
- A **minimal Spring Boot `jlink` runtime** can serve the application but may
  remove the tools and modules required for production diagnostics.
- A **diagnostic Spring Boot `jlink` runtime** keeps selected observability
  features while still avoiding a full JDK in the final image.

The pushback is important: do not use this example to claim that slim images are
bad. Use it to make diagnostic requirements explicit before deciding what to
remove from a runtime image.

For a complete Spring Boot container baseline that combines runtime sizing,
`jlink`, CDS, Project Leyden AOT cache, layered JARs, non-root execution, SBOM
generation, vulnerability scanning, and base-image review, continue with the
[all-in-one example](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).
